newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right slams "historic error" on Thomson-CSF.
newsitem.headline: French right slams "historic error" on Thomson-CSF.

text.p: The right-wing opposition on Saturday blasted the Socialist-led government's decision to halt the sale of electronics firm Thomson-CSF as a "historic error" that would relegate France to the minor league of Europe's defence industry.
Francois Fillon, technology minister in the previous centre-right government that launched the privatisation last year, said the sale of the government's 58 percent stake was strategically important.
He hinted that its cancellation might draw a direct response from conservative President Jacques Chirac.
"(Prime Minister) Lionel Jospin is committing an error, a historic error, for which he will be accountable to the French people," Fillon told Europe 1 radio.
The trend was towards defence industry alliances in Europe to head off competition from a heavily restructured U.S. defence industry which is undergoing a series of massive mergers, he said.
"As for us, we choose to turn in on ourselves and force Thomson to play in the second division."

Jospin's government announced on Friday, six weeks after being elected, that it had halted the privatisation process and would propose an alternative solution to build a French defence electronics conglomerate based on the company.
The state would retain a stake giving it ultimate decisionmaking power, Jospin's office said in a statement issued on the eve of a long Bastille Day holiday weekend.
Former conservative budget minister Alain Lamassoure said cancelling the selloff would deprive the government of billions of francs needed to recapitalise other state industries.

But the Communist party daily l'Humanite warmly praised the decision as "a breath of fresh air" proving the government was ready to carry out its electoral pledges. The Communists are junior partners in Jospin's "pink-red-green" coalition.
Fillon said the state, now battling to reduce its deficits to qualify for a European single currency, lacked the resources to invest in Thomson-CSF's growth.

Thomson-CSF, which makes radars, missiles and avionics, is one of Europe's largest defence electronics firms and seen as vital to France's ambitions to create a strong European defence industry able to meet tough U.S. competition.

Fillon said Chirac, who has made Thomson-CSF central to his ambitions for a restructured French defence industry, could intervene in the debate when he gives a traditional Bastille Day television interview on Monday.

"You have to distinguish between the question of economic management and the strategic aspects," he said. "This affair could have strategic consequences which I imagine the president will talk about."
Chirac, a Gaullist, was forced into uncomfortable power-sharing after Jospin's Socialist-led government won a stunning election victory on June 1.
But France's constitution still gives him considerable sway over foreign affairs and defence.

Le Figaro newspaper quoted unnamed sources close to Jospin on Saturday as saying he still envisaged a role for engineering giant Alcatel-Alsthom in Thomson-CSF, with the state retaining 40 percent and 20 percent remaining publicly quoted.
No one was available to comment at Jospin's office.
